name: The dissolution of the Self into a 'bundle of perceptions'
plain_explanation: Hume looked inward for some core 'self' beneath all his thoughts and feelings, and found nothing: only a constantly changing stream of particular perceptions (a sight, a sound, a feeling of pain) with no separate 'self' holding them together. He concluded the mind is really just a bundle of these perceptions, not a distinct thing that has them.
precise_definition: Hume denies any impression, and therefore any idea, of the self: 'when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other ... I never catch myself at any time without a perception'; he concludes we are 'nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions, which succeed each other with inconceivable rapidity, and are in a perpetual flux and movement.'
why_it_mattered: Russell regards this as 'of great importance' and largely correct: it eliminates the last surviving philosophical use of 'substance' from psychology (as Berkeley had eliminated it from physics), undermines theological claims to knowledge of an immortal 'soul,' and shows the subject/object distinction is not epistemologically fundamental.
historical_origin: Book I, Part IV, Section VI of the Treatise ('Of Personal Identity').
examples: Hume's introspective search, finding only 'heat or cold, light or shade, love or hatred, pain or pleasure' but never a bare 'self' apart from these
competing_positions: The traditional (Cartesian/scholastic) doctrine of the self as a persisting mental substance
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell endorses the core logical point -- that ideas of unperceived things (like the self, or one's own brain) can be defined in terms of perceived things, so nothing need be added beyond the bundle of perceptions -- as something 'any thoroughgoing empiricist must agree with.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly undermines theological claims to 'supposed knowledge of the soul.'
